title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
gist: A UK-funded war game on solar geoengineering governance ended with no deal, as US-China mistrust, disinformation and fossil-fuel-backed influence overrode climate science. The piece notes private firms like Stardust are pushing the technology while governments' posture is shifting toward research and strategic competition.

insights.claim: In the war game, the US and China each refused any deal constraining their research in the 'national interest' or favoring a rival; the US military player summarized it as worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Great-power rivalry, not climate science, is the likely driver of geoengineering governance outcomes.
insights.quote: worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China
insights.locator: The first session set the tone.

insights.claim: Mutual suspicion left all parties believing the others were racing to build capability even though China was not conducting experiments in the game, so misperception alone fueled an arms-race dynamic.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Misperception can trigger capability races without any real deployment, a dynamic like nuclear arms.
insights.quote: Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible
insights.locator: At the end of the session

insights.claim: Simulation results concluded that strategic competition and state sovereignty, not climate concerns, drove the simulations, and no deal was agreed despite multiple proposals.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Expect geoengineering policy to be framed as security policy.
insights.quote: strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns
insights.locator: At no point did the countries

insights.claim: A former British diplomat argues the threat of falling behind drives R&D but is not the same as deployment, and that the interdependence means it is not an inherently zero-sum game.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Counterview that competition may stop at research capability rather than deployment.
insights.locator: The threat of falling behind a rival

insights.claim: The organizers caution that simulations do not predict the future and depended on game design and players, many of whom lacked diplomatic or national security experience, and the UN forum setting may be less effective than small-group talks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A caveat on how much to infer from the outcome.
insights.quote: Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future.

insights.claim: Stardust Solutions, a US-Israeli startup, raised $60 million last year and in May released details of inventions it claims let humans dial down global temperature; its CEO says lobbying is getting easier as most policymakers are now aware of the technology.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Private capital is entering geoengineering, creating a lobbying and regulatory-risk landscape to track.

insights.claim: Elon Musk wrote in August that space satellites and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over, and SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering interventions.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Musk's advocacy links geoengineering to launch capacity and SpaceX optionality.

insights.claim: Policy is moving: two conservative US think-tank papers in March urged taking the lead against China using the term 'weather sovereignty', the UK MoD paid a consultancy for research, and the UK's first policy paper backed research but not deployment.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Governments are moving from taboo to strategic positioning, which could unlock public R&D funding.

insights.claim: Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, says governance decisions are needed within the next decade, not 15 years from now.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Scharf (as quoted by WIRED)
insights.so_what: Short timeline raises urgency for regulation and exposure to related companies.
insights.quote: It’s not 15 years from now; it’s in the next decade, easily.

themes.theme: Fossil fuel influence and science sidelined

insights.claim: A fossil-fuel-backed NGO in the game subtly obstructed talks and offered funding to the scientist to destroy her credibility, and several players noticed but did not call it out because it served their interests.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Fossil interests have an incentive to back geoengineering as it delays emissions cuts.

insights.claim: Scientific input was largely ignored in the game and a researcher described being ostracized for working on the technology, leaving little information on side effects.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Thin evidence base increases risk of poorly informed decisions.

insights.claim: Solar geoengineering would mimic volcanic cooling of half a degree or more but models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and stronger Atlantic tropical storms, and warming could rebound sharply if it stopped.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Uneven regional effects and termination shock create liability and conflict risk.
insights.quote: The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued
insights.locator: These technologies promise to reverse global warming
